content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Key-Value Stores Internal Architecture"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction to Key-Value Internals"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"Key-value stores are among the simplest yet most performant NoSQL databases available. Understanding their internal architecture is crucial for designing systems that require high throughput, low latency, and horizontal scalability. At their core, key-value stores optimize for fast lookups by mapping a unique key to a specific value without the overhead of relational schemas."},{"order":4,"type":"subheading","text":"Core Storage Engines: LSM-Trees vs. B-Trees"},{"order":5,"type":"paragraph","text":"Most modern key-value stores utilize Log-Structured Merge-trees (LSM-trees) rather than traditional B-trees. LSM-trees are optimized for write-heavy workloads by converting random writes into sequential disk writes, significantly reducing I/O bottlenecks."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"MemTable: An in-memory structure (typically a skip list or red-black tree) where all incoming writes are initially buffered and sorted by key."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Commit Log: An append-only disk log written simultaneously with the MemTable to ensure durability in case of system crashes."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"SSTables (Sorted String Tables): Immutable data files flushed to disk once the MemTable reaches a specific threshold."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Read and Write Path Mechanics"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"The efficiency of a key-value store relies heavily on how it handles the read and write paths. Writes are fast because they only touch the memory and append to the commit log. Reads, however, may require checking multiple components."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"Write Path: Client -> Commit Log (Disk) + MemTable (Memory)\nRead Path: MemTable -> Bloom Filters -> SSTables (Disk)"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"To prevent reads from scanning every SSTable on disk, key-value stores employ Bloom filters. A Bloom filter is a space-efficient probabilistic data structure used to test whether an element is definitely not in a set, or possibly in a set, saving unnecessary disk lookups."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Compaction Strategies"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Because SSTables are immutable, updates and deletes do not overwrite existing data; instead, they append new markers or values. Over time, this creates redundant data and requires compaction. Compaction processes background threads that merge multiple SSTables, discard deleted keys (tombstones), and purge outdated values to reclaim disk space."},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"By leveraging memory buffers, append-only logs, and LSM-tree structures with background compaction, key-value stores achieve predictable write performance and scalable read architectures suitable for modern distributed systems."}]
